stops.title: The whole graph
stops.text: 2,308 nodes and 13,261 edges. Top to bottom: why it exists, what the code does, what proves it. Every point is a row the loop wrote.

stops.title: Where it comes from
stops.text: A requirement has to come from somewhere it can be checked against: here, a named source.

stops.title: The requirement
stops.text: A requirement, a node of its own.

stops.title: The step that needs it
stops.text: A use case step binds it into a chain of cause and effect. Code is reached through the step, never from the requirement itself.

stops.title: Broken on purpose
stops.text: One break of the code, run alone against the tests. This test failed on it, so the requirement held.

stops.title: One decision
stops.text: The branch the break was made in.

stops.title: The code
stops.text: A method, the method that branch is in, reached through the step's own test.

stops.title: And one that got past
stops.text: No test caught this break. Either it changes nothing, and that has to be proven, or a test is missing.

stops.title: The readers
stops.text: Each large node outside the rings is one thing the harness tries to learn: 10 goals, 5 of them trained. Its rays go to what it reads. Solid has reached its goal, hollow has not, and a core in a shell is part way there or in doubt.

stops.title: Trying is not reaching
stops.text: Goal: who owns new code. It is trying, and it has not got there. The score below is against the plain rule it has to beat.

bp-agent.title: The agent at work
bp-agent.tip: What an agent does when someone asks it for a change. The tools below hold it to account; this sheet is the part only an agent can do.

bp-pass.title: One pass
bp-pass.tip: One command runs all of it, in this order. The numbers on the nodes come from a real pass on the kit's example, a small wallet and store in C#.

bp-breaking.title: Breaking the code
bp-breaking.tip: A coverage tool says a line ran. This asks whether any test would notice if the line were wrong. It never touches the live project; it works in a sandbox.

bp-requirements.title: The requirements, as data
bp-requirements.tip: The owner's words become a model a machine can check. Nothing here looks at whether the code works yet; this tests the requirements themselves.

bp-graph.title: The record, and 17 questions of it
bp-graph.tip: The graph is what the loop believes. Each criterion is one question asked of it, named for the mistake it would catch. A hole of ours fails the run; a hole of the owner's is a question.

bp-stats.title: The stats choose what's next
bp-stats.tip: Each pass measures itself. A stat nothing reads is a cost with no use, and the audit says so. The same shape sits one level up, where stats are the code, triggers the requirements and ticks the tests.

bp-tick.title: The standing tick
bp-tick.tip: A fresh agent with no memory, one item, the same stat measured before and after. Nothing starts a tick for you; schedule one or don't.

bp-learned.title: What learns, and has to earn it
bp-learned.tip: A graph network that proposes links, a small model that predicts which breaks get past the tests, and a list of goals. Each is measured against a plain rule on data it never saw, and stays off if it loses.

bp-measure.title: Does it help? On against off
bp-measure.tip: The honest measure. Two agents get the same prompt and only one gets the loop. The harness measures what they made, and graders who cannot see which is which judge it.

bp-ship.title: Shipping it
bp-ship.tip: The kit other developers install, and the public pages. A possible leak fails the build rather than warning about it.

bp-agents.title: Many agents at once
bp-agents.tip: The runtime underneath. Agents share a project through files, not a server, and a stuck worker asks instead of guessing. who.py says who is on what, from their own transcripts.

bp-cpp.title: The full C++ pseudocode
bp-cpp.tip: The whole system as pseudocode for a C++ reader, every function tagged with the real one it stands for.

harmony-2.title: 2. Trigger Fired

harmony-3.title: 3. Pick Names Work

harmony-4.title: 4. Goal Named

harmony-5.title: 5. Work Ran

harmony-6.title: 6. Stat Moved Back

harmony-7.title: 7. Lists Changed

harmony-8.title: 8. Growth Point

harmony-9.title: 9. Documents Flagged

harmony-10.title: 10. Graph Holds

tree.label: The guided tour
tree.tip: One real thread through the graph, from where a requirement comes from to the test that caught a break of it.

children.label: 1. The whole graph
children.tip: 2,308 nodes and 13,261 edges. Top to bottom: why it exists, what the code does, what proves it. Every point is a row the loop wrote.

children.label: 2. Where it comes from
children.tip: A requirement has to come from somewhere it can be checked against: here, a named source.

children.label: 3. The requirement
children.tip: A requirement, a node of its own.

children.label: 4. The step that needs it
children.tip: A use case step binds it into a chain of cause and effect. Code is reached through the step, never from the requirement itself.

children.label: 5. Its own test
children.tip: A test checks this requirement.

children.label: 6. Broken on purpose
children.tip: One break of the code, run alone against the tests. This test failed on it, so the requirement held.

children.label: 7. One decision
children.tip: The branch the break was made in.

children.label: 8. The code
children.tip: A method, the method that branch is in, reached through the step's own test.

children.label: 9. And one that got past
children.tip: No test caught this break. Either it changes nothing, and that has to be proven, or a test is missing.

children.label: 10. The readers
children.tip: Each large node outside the rings is one thing the harness tries to learn: 10 goals, 5 of them trained. Its rays go to what it reads. Solid has reached its goal, hollow has not, and a core in a shell is part way there or in doubt.

children.label: 11. Trying is not reaching
children.tip: Goal: who owns new code. It is trying, and it has not got there. The score below is against the plain rule it has to beat.

children.label: 12. The whole graph
children.tip: Fly anywhere: drag to orbit, scroll to zoom, W A S D to move. Point at a node to see what kind it is.

children.label: Watch it run

children.label: All the floors
children.tip: Every part of the system, each floor a Blueprint.

children.label: The agent at work
children.tip: What an agent does when someone asks it for a change. The tools below hold it to account; this sheet is the part only an agent can do.

children.label: One pass
children.tip: One command runs all of it, in this order. The numbers on the nodes come from a real pass on the kit's example, a small wallet and store in C#.

children.label: Breaking the code
children.tip: A coverage tool says a line ran. This asks whether any test would notice if the line were wrong. It never touches the live project; it works in a sandbox.

children.label: The requirements, as data
children.tip: The owner's words become a model a machine can check. Nothing here looks at whether the code works yet; this tests the requirements themselves.

children.label: The record, and 17 questions of it
children.tip: The graph is what the loop believes. Each criterion is one question asked of it, named for the mistake it would catch. A hole of ours fails the run; a hole of the owner's is a question.

children.label: The stats choose what's next
children.tip: Each pass measures itself. A stat nothing reads is a cost with no use, and the audit says so. The same shape sits one level up, where stats are the code, triggers the requirements and ticks the tests.

children.label: The standing tick
children.tip: A fresh agent with no memory, one item, the same stat measured before and after. Nothing starts a tick for you; schedule one or don't.

children.label: What learns, and has to earn it
children.tip: A graph network that proposes links, a small model that predicts which breaks get past the tests, and a list of goals. Each is measured against a plain rule on data it never saw, and stays off if it loses.

children.label: Does it help? On against off
children.tip: The honest measure. Two agents get the same prompt and only one gets the loop. The harness measures what they made, and graders who cannot see which is which judge it.

children.label: Shipping it
children.tip: The kit other developers install, and the public pages. A possible leak fails the build rather than warning about it.

children.label: Many agents at once
children.tip: The runtime underneath. Agents share a project through files, not a server, and a stuck worker asks instead of guessing. who.py says who is on what, from their own transcripts.

Slide 1 of 26: TNT Tools · internal training manual

How to use AI for games

The words on this slide

How to use AI for games

Adapted for Heavy Iron. Requirements first, tested by AI, so nothing is a guess.

BUG REPORT · FOUND BY AI · CHECK IT YOURSELF

UNREAL ENGINE 5.7

Unreal’s own SemVer class, in its C# tooling, throws on the SemVer spec’s own example.

SPEC

semver.org , rule 9, lists 1.0.0-x-y-z.-- as a valid version

CODE

Engine/Source/Programs/Shared/EpicGames.Core/SemVer.cs , in the 5.7 install

TRY

var v = SemVer.Parse("1.0.0-x-y-z.--"); v.CompareTo(v); // ArgumentOutOfRangeException

TESTS

The class has 2 tests, and both pass.

Three faults like this one, in code you can read, and how to check each

What the speaker says

This is how we use AI at TNT Tools: our internal training manual, adapted for you. It opens on one fault you can check in a couple of minutes with the engine you already have. The SemVer spec, rule 9, lists 1.0.0-x-y-z.-- among its valid versions. Unreal Engine 5.7’s own SemVer class, in EpicGames.Core, parses it, and then throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException when it compares that version with itself. Any pre-release ending in a hyphen does the same. The class has 2 tests, and both pass. An AI agent found it by reading the class against the spec, rule by rule, while writing down what the class must do; re-run on the installed 5.7 source on 3 November. Slide 3 has three faults like it, each with the public page that shows it. Behind this slide: The real graph of osu!’s scoring rules: 1,062 nodes, drawn from the store the loop wrote.

The new tool

A skill that installs itself, and puts requirements first on every build

You ask Claude to build something. Before any code, it writes down what the thing must do, and you sign that off.

1

REQUIREMENTS

Write it down

What it must do, each line saying where it came from. Anything missing becomes a question for you.

2

Plan the play

Who does what, step by step, and what should happen at each step. The main path at least.

GATE

REVIEW 1

I reviewed it

3

CODE

Build, step by step

Each change says which step it serves, and why.

GATE

REVIEW 2

Read the intent, not the diff

What it meant to do at each step, and the problem each change solves. A change that serves no step is flagged.

4

EVERY RUN

Fly through it

A 3D map of what was built and why: requirements, steps and code, to fly through at the end.

Install it, in plain words

2

What the speaker says

This is the tool. Claude installs it as a skill, and from then on every time you ask it to build something it starts with the requirements, not the code. First it writes down what the thing must do, each line citing where it came from, and turns every gap into a question for you. Then it writes the use cases: who does what, step by step, and what should happen, the main path at least. You read that one page and press I reviewed it; no code is written for any other version. While it codes, every change names the use case step it serves and says why. The second review is of those intentions, not the diff: a step with no intent, a change with no step and a change that solves no problem are each flagged. At the end of every run there is a fly-through, a 3D map of the requirements, the steps and the code.

Three faults an AI found by reading code against its own spec

The words on this slide

Check each one yourself

Three faults an AI found by reading code against its own spec

UNREAL ENGINE 5.7 · SemVer.cs

Comparing the spec’s own example version with itself throws.

1.0.0-alpha-10 sorts above 1.0.0-alpha-9 . The spec says below.

The rule: semver.org , rules 9 and 11

UNREAL ENGINE 5.7 · JsonObject.cs

Equals throws NullReferenceException on any object with a null field, even x.Equals(x) .

Try {"a":null} .

The rule: Microsoft’s Object.Equals : x.Equals(x) is true, and Equals must not throw

OSU!, OPEN SOURCE · ScoreProcessor.cs

TotalScoreWithoutMods reads 1,000,000 before the first hit, while TotalScore reads 0.

Its doc says it is the points awarded.

The rule: its own doc comment, on GitHub

How: an AI agent read each class against its spec or its docs, rule by rule, while writing down what the class must do. Each fault was then run on the code as shipped. Nothing in the targets was changed or added.

Each fault, and how to re-run it

3

What the speaker says

Three faults on code outside our own project, each against a rule anyone can read. Unreal Engine 5.7’s SemVer class, in EpicGames.Core under Engine/Source/Programs, throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException when it compares 1.0.0-x-y-z.--, a version the spec lists as valid in rule 9, with itself; and it treats a hyphen as a separator, so 1.0.0-alpha-10 sorts above 1.0.0-alpha-9 where rule 11 puts it below. Its JsonObject’s Equals throws NullReferenceException on any object holding a null field, even when compared with itself, where Microsoft’s published contract says x.Equals(x) is true and Equals must not throw. Both were re-run on the installed 5.7 source on 3 November. osu! is a shipped open-source rhythm game: at commit 845336e, TotalScoreWithoutMods reads 1,000,000 right after ApplyBeatmap while TotalScore reads 0, and the field’s doc comment says it is the points awarded without mod multipliers; that one was re-run on a fresh clone of that commit on 3 November. An agent found all three by reading each class against its rules while writing the requirements; the planted bugs on the next slide did not find them. Behind this slide: osu!’s real graph.

slide-flatter.head:
Slide 4 of 26: Why the tests did not catch it

A line that runs is not a line that is checked

The words on this slide

Why the tests did not catch it

A line that runs is not a line that is checked

COVERAGE

90%

of SemVer.cs’s lines run when its 2 tests run. Coverage counts lines run. It cannot tell whether a test would notice that a line is wrong.

PLANT A BUG, RUN THE TESTS

30

of the 236 planted bugs that compiled and changed the program left every test green, each tried alone. Our count, by mutation testing: change one thing, like a < into <= , and see if any test fails.

Try one yourself: make JsonObject.Equals answer true for anything. No test that passed before fails, in either test project that uses the class.

Published, not ours: coverage is only weakly tied to how many planted bugs tests catch, once suite size is allowed for. Inozemtseva and Holmes, ICSE 2014 .

What was tested, and how

4

What the speaker says

The faults were found by reading. This slide is about why the tests let them through. On Unreal Engine 5.7’s SemVer class, which follows the public Semantic Versioning 2.0.0 spec and has 2 tests, a coverage tool reported 90% of lines and 85% of branches run. Coverage only says a line ran. So we planted bugs, the standard way called mutation testing: change one thing in the code, such as a less-than into a less-than-or-equal, a check removed, or a method made to answer a constant, then run the tests and see if any fails. We made 246 such changes, one at a time, each in its own copy. 236 counted (the rest did not compile, or compiled to the same program as the original): the tests caught 206 and left 30 green, and 14 of those 30 were on lines the coverage tool counts as run. That count is ours, and the recipe to re-run it is in the manual. The example on the slide you can check with the engine you have: we made JsonObject’s Equals answer true for anything, and no test that passed on the clean copy failed, in EpicGames.Core.Tests or in UnrealBuildTool.Tests. The general point is not ours: Inozemtseva and Holmes measured it on large Java projects and found coverage only low to moderately tied to how many planted bugs a suite catches once its size is allowed for. Behind this slide: every planted bug in osu!’s scoring rules. Red: no test caught it.

slide-numbers.head:
Slide 5 of 26: Measured, in plain words

What one run found about the tests themselves

The words on this slide

Measured, in plain words

What one run found about the tests themselves

7 of 16

rules we took from the SemVer spec for this class have no test about them, including every rule on which strings are valid. Read its 2 tests in SemVerTests.cs beside semver.org.

3 questions

the spec leaves unsaid, such as how the class should refuse a bad string. They go to the code’s owner as questions. The tool never answers them itself.

206 of 236

planted bugs in SemVer.cs made a test fail, counting those that compiled and changed the program. In JsonObject.cs, 299 of 429. In osu!’s scoring, 286 of 536, against the 151 tests we ran. Our counts.

13 min

for the whole SemVer run, each planted bug built and tested in its own copy, never in the live project. osu! took 74: a change to a constructor rebuilds the game.

Where each number comes from

5

What the speaker says

These are the three public trials of 30 October, read in plain words. The first number you can check by reading: Unreal Engine 5.7’s SemVer class has 2 tests, and of the 16 requirements we took from the Semantic Versioning 2.0.0 spec for it, 7 have no test about them, including every rule about which strings are valid; which test is about what was our reading of each test, written before any bug was planted. The 3 questions are the model’s own: the spec says what is valid, not how a class refuses a bad string, and nobody has said which; they go to the owner, never settled by the tool. The planted-bug counts leave out changes that did not compile or compiled to the same program as the original. osu!’s count is what three test files hold, 151 tests, and reads low for the game as a whole: its full test project crashed on this machine on the clean copy too. The SemVer pass took 765 seconds, about 13 minutes, at low priority on a busy machine. The faults themselves are on slide 3. Requirements make requirements

It extracts new requirements from the ones you have

Automatic

Each use case step needs something. What no requirement provides becomes a new one, marked inferred, and goes to the owner as a question. On SemVer it inferred 3 beside the 16 the spec states; on osu!’s scoring, none.

Complete in, accurate out

The more complete the requirements, the more accurate the prompt built from them. Start with the ones that run through the most code.

Epic to code: run, results held

What the speaker says

The first card is the mechanism: it walks each use case, and when a step needs a condition that nothing provides, it marks an inferred requirement and sends it to the owner as a question, never as a decision. slide-breaks.head:
Slide 10 of 26: Planting bugs on purpose

Mutation testing: every decision, changed every way

The words on this slide

Planting bugs on purpose

Mutation testing: every decision, changed every way

Conditions

negated, made true, made false

Operators

< to <=, equality swapped, && to ||, arithmetic swapped

Values

a number plus one, a bool flipped, a text emptied, an argument defaulted

Structure

ternary arms swapped, an else removed, a statement removed, an early return

When no test catches a planted bug, there are only two honest answers

It is the same program

The change did not change the program: proven when the compiled IL is identical. Otherwise it needs a written reason, which lapses when that code changes.

A test is missing

So write it. Each requirement’s claim on its code is pinned to that code’s fingerprint, so an edited line reopens the claim. Our own “same program” calls have been wrong before, and tests now hold those cases.

Behind: planted bugs up close. Each point is one change to one decision.

What a planted bug is, and when it changes nothing

10

What the speaker says

This is mutation testing: each planted bug is one small change to the code, and a test should fail because of it. Up to 24 planted bugs a statement, one of each kind first. One limit on every: until this week the C# adapter skipped overloads, operators and property bodies without saying so, and it still does not walk a field's value or an indexer, which the report now names; slide 15 has the numbers. A planted bug that every test passes is either a missing test or the same program. Same program is proven by comparing compiled code, Trivial Compiler Equivalence from Papadakis and others, 2015. Anything else needs a reason in writing, and a declared equivalent that a test ever kills is a hole, not a pass. Behind this slide: one stretch of the planted bugs up close: each point is one change to one decision.

slide-chain.head:
Slide 11 of 26: Checking Claude’s reasoning

Claude writes its reasoning as a chain; the graph checks every step

The words on this slide

Checking Claude’s reasoning

Claude writes its reasoning as a chain; the graph checks every step

says: "A limited line sells its quantity and is then sold out" cites: [W-3, Store.Buy]

Where it meets the code: the step becomes a node citing two nodes already there. A branch of that method maps to that requirement, so the two join, 2 links apart.

Grounded: a cite that is not there fails the run. Joined: what a step cites must connect within 4 links. Read for truth: a reader holding the whole source reads every step for what is wrong. A real step once said “or” where the code needs both, and grounding alone passed it.

1 of 1

owner’s question this chain never reached

OWNER: where it is stated

W-3: the requirement

A use case step needs it

Claude’s step cites both

Store.Buy: the code

A branch of it maps to W-3

A planted bug in that branch

The test that caught it

The chain checks, and what they do not check yet

11

What the speaker says

This is how we go after hallucination. When Claude finishes a change it writes down, step by step, why the change does what the requirements ask. A chain is a written argument it produces on purpose, like showing your work; it is not a recording of the model's private thinking. Here is how it meets the code. The chain and every step become nodes in the same graph as the code. Each step has cites edges to the requirement and the method it stands on. A cite to something that is not a node fails the run, so a made-up requirement or a method the code does not have cannot pass. Then the graph walks from one cite to the next: here W-3 and Store.Buy meet because a branch of that method maps to W-3, two links apart. If they do not meet within 4 links, the step is reported. An owner's question no step reached is listed as a blind spot; this chain never reached W-4, what a refused purchase does to the stock. The step and the picture are from the kit's example, which you can run yourself: the chain was added to a copy of it and the whole loop run, and it held. Be precise about the limit of the grounding: it checks what each claim stands on, not whether the claim is true; that is the job of the full-source review, which reads every step against the whole source and is on by default, and no check yet walks on from a step to whether the code it stands on is tested, though the links are there, as the picture shows. It removes the hallucination that invents a source; it cannot promise to remove all of it. And one real step is the proof: a fresh reviewer found it said or where the code needs both. It was grounded and joined, and it was still wrong.

The words on this slide

The record

The graph remembers; closed means no “may” is left

MUST

Authored requirements

The owner wrote them. Each must hold, and a test must notice when it does not.

MAY

Inferred requirements

What the chain needs and nobody wrote. Only the owner settles each one.

What the speaker says

When to use it, and what it is not yet

The words on this slide

Honest limits

When to use it, and what it is not yet

Use it when

many changes will touch the same code

a rule must still hold after the tenth edit

agents run long, across context windows

it is a one-off prompt or a quick script

Built for large, complicated systems. To build something simple, do not use it. It has not been measured on large systems yet.

A prototype

Version 0.1. Bugs are planted in C# and Python only: no C++ or Blueprint adapter yet. On Unreal’s SemVer.cs its C# adapter first saw 35 of 68 statements, and the report did not say so. Fixed, with planted tests.

A thin graph misleads

A full pass takes time

13 minutes for SemVer’s 246 planted bugs, 74 for osu!’s 563.

Verdict run(Model& m, bool selfImprove = true) { Breaks b = Mutate(m.code); // one compile Results r = RunEachAlone(b, m.tests); Graph g = KnowledgeGraph(m, r); Holes h = Criteria(g); // 18 checks if (self_improve_on(m, selfImprove)) { Row row = PassStats(m).collect(); // 44 stats MorphLog(m).add(row); auto fired = improvement::fires(rules, log); Print(NextImprovement(log, fired).picks()); } return h.ours.empty() ? HOLDS : OPEN; }

// One tick. A fresh agent, one item, no memory. void Tick() { Start s = loop_tick::start(); // the lock if (s.stopped || s.busy || s.idle) return; if (s.epochStarts) Brainstorm(); // every 12 RunSelftests(); // red = item telemetry_audit(); // unread = item Item i = Choose(improvement::check(), board); Stat before = i.stat.Measure(); i.Do(); // one change Stat after = i.stat.Measure(); if (s.epochEnds) { run_plan::decide(); // parts on or off improvement::graph(); // did it work? } loop_tick::finish(i, before, after, worth); }

The same shape, one level up: stats are its code, triggers its requirements, ticks its tests. Three ticks worth “no” in a row and it sleeps until something changes.

The recursive graph, in plain words

22

What the speaker says

The toolkit is written in Python; this is pseudo C++ for a C++ audience, and the lower-case names are the real ones in the code: self_improve_on, improvement fires and check, loop_tick start and finish, telemetry_audit, run_plan decide, improvement graph. Left: one pass, which is what an agent runs. If self-improvement is on, it writes a row and prints the stats' picks. Right: one tick, the standing job. A fresh agent, no memory, chooses one item: a red selftest first, then an unread stat, then a fired trigger, then the board. It measures the same stat before and after. Every 12 ticks is an epoch: the first tick brainstorms, the last benchmarks, re-decides which parts run and asks whether the improvements worked. The improvement graph is checked the way the requirement graph is. Behind this slide: Inside the tool's own graph.

A part that does not beat a plain rule is switched off

The words on this slide

Experimental · What we switched off

A part that does not beat a plain rule is switched off

Every learned part had to beat a simple rule that does not learn. The ones that lost are off, and the record says when one may come back.

OFF · THE GRAPH NEURAL NETWORK (GNN)

Who owns new code 0.65 vs 0.72: on the tool’s own code it lost to a plain rule, so it is off.

Retired on 3 November. One rule stays in the switch file: when a project’s graph reaches 5,000 entities it is tried again, and must win by more than 0.02 on code it has not seen. A score of 1.0 means the right answer is always ranked first.

OFF · ITS OTHER JOBS

Which test catches which planted bug is now read off the test runs, and a bug that changes nothing is proven by the compiled code. Nothing is left to guess.

OFF · TWO MORE

A learned pick of a step’s requirements lost to plain similarity, and neither is used: the author binds each step’s requirements, and the model rules refuse a step that binds none. A learned order for running the planted bugs was retired, because the break-order head does that job.

The graph network’s whole story, and its numbers

24

What the speaker says

Every learned part of the tool was held to one rule: it must beat a plain rule that does not learn, on code it has not seen, or it is switched off. The graph neural network lost. On the tool's own code it ranked the right owner of new code at 0.65 against the plain rule's 0.72, so it was retired on 3 November. One rule stays in the switch file: when a project's graph reaches 5,000 entities it is tried again, and it must win by more than 0.02. Its other jobs need no guessing any more: which test catches which planted bug is read off the test runs themselves, and a bug that changes nothing is proven by comparing compiled code. Two other learned parts are off as well: the pick of a step's requirements lost to plain similarity, and neither is used now, because the author binds each step's requirements and the model rules refuse a step that binds none, and the learned order for running the planted bugs, which did beat its plain rule, was retired because the break-order head shown next does that job. Switching off what does not beat a simple rule is the point: the record says why each part is off and what would wake it.

The words on this slide

Experimental · What does the job now

Two small checking heads, each beating the best plain rule

A head is one weighted sum of four measured signals, such as how alike two texts are and the words they share, trained on the project’s own record. Cheap, and its weights can be read.

ON · THE OWNER HEAD

Which use case step owns a piece of code, before it has tests

0.549 right first time, against 0.479 for matching words, the best plain rule. Measured on 71 places in one feature of our own game.

ON · THE BREAK-ORDER HEAD

Which planted bugs to run first

54% of the bugs no test catches land in the first quarter of the run, against 21% for the best plain rule; random order would find one in four. On 1,335 planted bugs in the same feature.

And what needs no learning: which test catches which bug is read off the runs, and code links to a use case step by running that step’s own tests.

How each was tested, and what replaced what

25

What the speaker says

What does the graph network's jobs now. Two small checking heads, each a linear model: one weighted sum of four measured signals, trained on the project's own record, so it is cheap and anyone can read its weights. Both were held to the same rule as the network, and both passed it with their bars committed before the run. The owner head says which use case step owns a piece of code before that code has tests: it was right first time 0.549 of the time, against 0.479 for matching words, the best plain rule, on 71 places in one feature of our own game. The break-order head decides which planted bugs to run first, so the ones no test catches show up early: 54% of them landed in the first quarter of the run, against 21% for the best plain rule, where a random order would find one in four; that was on 1,335 planted bugs in the same feature. Both are on one feature of our own, not on public code, so read them as a first measurement. The rest needs no learning at all: which test catches which bug is read off the test runs, and code is linked to a use case step by running that step's own tests.

Where it comes from

A mutation of the self-improvement loop of ARC3, an agent harness we built for a benchmark of puzzle games, and that loop's failure is why it distrusts its own numbers. Ours is internal, so this version was made for you.

How new it is

A small edge, for now

Where it comes from, and what it measured there

26

What the speaker says

This is the method we use ourselves at TNT Tools. The harness comes from ARC3, an agent harness we built for a benchmark of puzzle games. That project's autonomous self-improvement run went 16 days and found nothing that generalized: a counter that could be gamed rose while the honest number stayed flat. That failure is why every stat here must have a reader, a control and a fresh reviewer. As harnesses improve this will become more common knowledge, so the edge is small and it is for now. Our graph is shared across the team as a retrieval store; this version is not networked, and you could add that in whatever way suits your network. goals.head:
The goals

The readers

Each large node outside the rings is one thing the loop tries to learn: 10 goals, 5 of them trained. Trying is not reaching: solid has reached its goal, a core in a shell is part way there or in doubt, hollow has not got there, and a faint ring is only planned.

  • Who owns new code: Has not reached it.
  • Which tests catch a break: Reached on 1 of 2.
  • Which steps carry a requirement: Has not reached it.
  • Which breaks change nothing: Reached, but doubted.
  • Which breaks will get past the tests: Reached its goal.
  • Where to add a test: Uses another goal's model.
  • A second opinion on every claim: Planned.
  • What a change will break, before the run: Planned, waits for a second pass on changed code (HD-8's data), since the truth is what a change really broke; no station asks for it yet.
  • Which methods change together: Planned.
  • Which action moves which stat: Planned, waits for 20 measured outcomes (0 in improvement/graph_stats.jsonl on 11-03; the stations' 33 measured results are another record, of mechanisms against bars).

So far

  • Graph network reached its goal on 1 of 6 results; small model on the break's features reached its goal on 4 of 4 results (2 of them doubted) (a pattern to test: 10 results from 2 projects).
  • 3 of 10 results change with the random seed alone, so no single run settles one (a pattern to test: 10 results from 2 projects).
  • Giving a goal more of the graph to read helped by more than the bar in 0 of 6 tries (an anecdote: 6 results).
  • Goals where each answer belongs to about one source, in a sparse table, beat a plain rule far more often than the rest. That says where plain rules are weak, not where work is saved (right 80% of the time against a 48% base, on 44 goals across 5 graphs, and 6 of 7 on goals sealed before they ran (an anecdote at that size)).
  • No rule was found that picks the goals which save work. All 60 of the best candidates were chance or anecdote (52 goals with a measured saving, across 5 domains).
  • Ordering tests by a plain rule already saves most of what ordering them can. A learned order beat it on only 2 of 10 goals (10 goals, 31% against 33% saved).
  • The graph offers these next, relations nothing predicts yet: documented in (390 links), checked by (134 links), links to (64 links), asserts (55 links), stated by (45 links).

concept-goals.head:
The goals

The readers

Each large node outside the rings is one thing the loop tries to learn: 10 goals, 5 of them trained. Trying is not reaching: solid has reached its goal, a core in a shell is part way there or in doubt, hollow has not got there, and a faint ring is only planned.

  • Who owns new code: Has not reached it.
  • Which tests catch a break: Reached on 1 of 2.
  • Which steps carry a requirement: Has not reached it.
  • Which breaks change nothing: Reached, but doubted.
  • Which breaks will get past the tests: Reached its goal.
  • Where to add a test: Uses another goal's model.
  • A second opinion on every claim: Planned.
  • What a change will break, before the run: Planned, waits for a second pass on changed code (HD-8's data), since the truth is what a change really broke; no station asks for it yet.
  • Which methods change together: Planned.
  • Which action moves which stat: Planned, waits for 20 measured outcomes (0 in improvement/graph_stats.jsonl on 11-03; the stations' 33 measured results are another record, of mechanisms against bars).

So far

  • Graph network reached its goal on 1 of 6 results; small model on the break's features reached its goal on 4 of 4 results (2 of them doubted) (a pattern to test: 10 results from 2 projects).
  • 3 of 10 results change with the random seed alone, so no single run settles one (a pattern to test: 10 results from 2 projects).
  • Giving a goal more of the graph to read helped by more than the bar in 0 of 6 tries (an anecdote: 6 results).
  • Goals where each answer belongs to about one source, in a sparse table, beat a plain rule far more often than the rest. That says where plain rules are weak, not where work is saved (right 80% of the time against a 48% base, on 44 goals across 5 graphs, and 6 of 7 on goals sealed before they ran (an anecdote at that size)).
  • No rule was found that picks the goals which save work. All 60 of the best candidates were chance or anecdote (52 goals with a measured saving, across 5 domains).
  • Ordering tests by a plain rule already saves most of what ordering them can. A learned order beat it on only 2 of 10 goals (10 goals, 31% against 33% saved).
  • The graph offers these next, relations nothing predicts yet: documented in (390 links), checked by (134 links), links to (64 links), asserts (55 links), stated by (45 links).

help.head:
Help

How to use this page

Pick anything in the tree on the left and the camera flies there, with its page open down here. Pick it again, or use the bar at the top of this page, and the page closes. Flying freely leaves the page as it is.

Flying

  • Drag to orbit. Scroll or pinch to zoom. W, A, S, D fly, Q and E go down and up.
  • N and P move to the next and previous item in this part of the tree.
  • Point at a node to see what kind it is. Click or tap it to open its page: the data behind it, then what that kind of thing is. Click a slide or a reader in the world to go to it.
  • The question mark key opens this page.

The tree

  • Up and down arrows move, right opens, left closes, Enter flies. Home and End go to the ends, and typing a letter jumps to it.
  • The filter box finds anything by its words.

The levels and the chain

  • The levels are four graphs you can fly between: the tool pointed at a game, at its own code, at its learned parts and at its own improvement. A world too big to draw whole is thinned, and the line under the title says how many nodes of how many are drawn.
  • Harmony is a path of ten stops, one per link of the chain from a worsening stat to the documents that describe it. Each stop says PASS, FAIL or NOT WIRED from the last recorded run.

Links

  • Every item has its own address, so a slide or a goal can be sent as a link. Copy link is on the bar of this page.
  • A link in a page to something in the tree flies there. A link to the full manual, a concept page or the deck opens a new tab.

On a touch screen

The text of a tooltip is here, and on the page of the item you pick. A long press on a control shows it too.

  • Contents: Shows or hides the tree of everything you can fly to.
  • ‹: The tour's previous stop.
  • Tour: Start or stop the guided tour along one real thread through the graph.
  • ›: The tour's next stop.
  • Whole graph: Fly back to see the whole graph. The page stays as it is.
  • ?: Help: how to fly, and where the manual is.
  • Hide: Hide the tree, for more room.
  • Page: Shows or hides the page for the selected item. Up and down arrows change its height.
  • Previous: The previous item in this part of the tree.
  • Next: The next item in this part of the tree.
  • Copy link: Copy a link that opens on this item.

Where the rest is

  • The whole manual, as one document.
  • The deck, as slides.
  • The first page.

world-games.head:
Level 1 of 4

Requirements about a game

The tool's requirements for a small game feature, the code that meets them, every break tried on that code and the tests that caught it. It is the graph the rest of this page first showed.

What is drawn

Drawing all 2,308 nodes and all 13,261 lines.

  • 39 requirements, 82 methods, 57 tests
  • 1,473 breaks tried on the code: 1,283 caught by a test, 52 got past every test, and 138 have no verdict (they did not build, or no test covers their file). The last two are the red nodes.

What the level above is checking

The level above is the tool's own code (the next world up). Its requirements say what the tool must do to a graph like this one: find every decision, break it every way it knows, and say which tests caught each break. The same method breaks the tool's own code: 1,639 breaks were tried, 989 were caught, 648 got past every test and 2 have no verdict.

Readers

The goals and the stats are the loop reading itself. They stand round the first world, and both are one click from here: the goals and the stats. Its passes write the stats, and the goals learn from this graph.

world-tool.head:
Level 2 of 4

Requirements about the tool itself

The same kind of graph, drawn for the tool's own code: its requirements, its methods, every break tried on them and the tests that caught each one.

What is drawn

Drawing 1,800 of 2,365 nodes and 3,852 of 6,272 lines. The rest are thinned breaks and decisions; every red break is drawn.

  • 20 requirements, 38 methods, 131 tests
  • 1,639 breaks tried on the code: 989 caught by a test, 648 got past every test, and 2 have no verdict (they did not build, or no test covers their file). The last two are the red nodes.

What the level above is checking

The level above is the six learned parts. They are networks trained on graphs like this one, to guess which requirement owns new code, which breaks change nothing and where to add a test. They are held to requirements by the same method, so their code has a graph too: 1,816 breaks were tried on it, 1,174 were caught, 642 got past every test and 0 have no verdict.

Readers

The goals and the stats are the loop reading itself. They stand round the first world, and both are one click from here: the goals and the stats. The stats are written by passes on every level, this one included.

world-learned.head:
Level 3 of 4

Requirements about the learned parts

The same kind of graph for the six small networks that learn from the other graphs, with the jobs they do and the stats they read joined in.

What is drawn

Drawing 1,800 of 3,298 nodes and 3,218 of 8,863 lines. The rest are thinned breaks and decisions; every red break is drawn.

  • 48 requirements, 67 methods, 90 tests
  • 1,816 breaks tried on the code: 1,174 caught by a test, 642 got past every test, and 0 have no verdict (they did not build, or no test covers their file). The last two are the red nodes.
  • 6 jobs a network does
  • 144 stats they read

What the level above is checking

The level above is the improvement model. It reads the stats that every level writes, this one included, and asks of each: is it read, and does it trigger something? It holds 33 requirements, 5 of whose triggers have fired and 4 of those have no answer from a tick yet.

Readers

The goals and the stats are the loop reading itself. They stand round the first world, and both are one click from here: the goals and the stats. This world is what the goals about the learned parts are measured on.

world-improve.head:
Level 4 of 4

Requirements about improving the loop

The registry of what each stat must trigger: a requirement per stat, the action it asks for, and the ticks that answered. It is a graph built from the registry and the tick ledger.

What is drawn

Drawing all 90 nodes and all 71 lines.

  • 33 requirements, one per stat, each saying what a pattern in the stat must trigger
  • 5 triggers fired on the last passes, 4 with no answer yet
  • 5 ticks on the ledger, 0 with a measured outcome
  • its own health, read on 2026-10-30 09:24: 2 banked records, learnable not yet

What the level above is checking

There is no fourth world. The improvement model writes its own health back as stats (stats that are read, triggers that are answered, ticks that named their stat), and the same registry watches them, so the tower closes on itself. The rules that check the other three levels have not been run on this one: it is drawn from the registry and the tick ledger, and not from a model they have walked.

Readers

The goals and the stats are the loop reading itself. They stand round the first world, and both are one click from here: the goals and the stats. The stats are written by passes on every level, this one included.

worlds.head:
The recursion

The tool, pointed at itself, three times

The tool holds code to written requirements by breaking the code on purpose. Pointed at a game, that is level 1. Pointed at its own code it is level 2, at the networks it contains level 3, and at the way it improves itself level 4. Each is a real graph read from the store the tool wrote, standing in space where you can fly to it.

  • Level 1: Requirements about a game. Drawing all 2,308 nodes and all 13,261 lines.
  • Level 2: Requirements about the tool itself. Drawing 1,800 of 2,365 nodes and 3,852 of 6,272 lines. The rest are thinned breaks and decisions; every red break is drawn.
  • Level 3: Requirements about the learned parts. Drawing 1,800 of 3,298 nodes and 3,218 of 8,863 lines. The rest are thinned breaks and decisions; every red break is drawn.
  • Level 4: Requirements about improving the loop. Drawing all 90 nodes and all 71 lines.

Across the four worlds 5,998 of 8,061 nodes are drawn. A world too big to draw whole is thinned, every break no test caught is kept, and each page says how many of how many.

A world with no graph still stands here and says why it is empty. None is empty today: all four have a graph.

harmony.head:
Harmony

Do the stats, the learned parts and the graphs work together?

One stat is made worse on a scratch copy of the tools, and the change is followed through ten links. 8 of 10 hold. 2 is not wired: link 5, work ran, link 8, growth point. None fails.

  • 1. Stat Moved PASS The worse value is in the log, and the trend reads it as worsening.
  • 2. Trigger Fired PASS An improvement requirement on the stat fires.
  • 3. Pick Names Work PASS The pick of the next work names its area because of the stat.
  • 4. Goal Named PASS The Stats List names the goal that reads the stat, and a requirement that reads it.
  • 5. Work Ran NOT WIRED The work the pick named is launched through the tick's launcher, and its end, or its failure, is on file.
  • 6. Stat Moved Back PASS The tick that targeted the stat has a measured outcome: the stat's own value before and after.
  • 7. Lists Changed PASS The Goals List and the Stats List are rewritten by the tick that finished.
  • 8. Growth Point NOT WIRED The growth page is rebuilt by the tick and draws the stat's new readings.
  • 9. Documents Flagged PASS The tick says which documents describe the stat, from the graph.
  • 10. Graph Holds PASS One graph of the tool itself holds the stat, the goal that uses it and the documents, joined by edges.

Every link that is wired has a plant, one change to the scratch copy that breaks only that link. 8 of 8 plants turned their link off PASS, and 0 links turned red that were not meant to.

Read from the record made on 2026-11-03 19:08 by harmony.py, and refused if any of the 9 tools it ran has changed since. Run it again: py -X utf8 autobot/harmony.py --prove --record. The worse values in the evidence are planted for the run on a scratch copy; they are not results about the learned parts. A link says NOT WIRED when nothing calls the step for this stat; it says FAIL when something does and the step goes wrong.

growth.head:
Growth

The growth charts, in words

How the closed loop has grown, drawn only from the dated records it keeps about itself. Every point is a reading in a log row that carries a date, and nothing is estimated, interpolated or filled. A line is drawn only through 3 or more readings, and is broken wherever what was counted changed (the kinds of break tried, the criteria checked). With fewer readings the page shows the readings and says so. Every reading here was taken between 10-29 12:02 and 10-31 22:07, so most of what the loop records has few readings; that is itself the finding.

  • 796 dated points drawn
  • 44 logs read
  • 66 series long enough for a line
  • 14 series with one or two readings, shown as dots
  • 31 series flat
  • 7 series fell

sections.publiccode:
On code you can read for yourself

Three trials on 30 October 2026, on code outside our own project: two parts of Unreal Engine's own C# and the scoring rules of a shipped open-source game. Every number below was measured on these runs, and every defect was reproduced by running it. No test and no product code was written for any target: only the requirements model, and /// CHECKS: comments in a scratch copy of the tests. Findings were proven with throwaway calls that are not part of any result.

What was tested

  • Unreal Engine 5.7, EpicGames.Core/SemVer.cs. Requirements: the public Semantic Versioning 2.0.0 spec, every numbered rule either mapped or excluded with a reason. Tests: EpicGames.Core.Tests, 2 of them on this class.
  • Unreal Engine 5.7, EpicGames.Core/JsonObject.cs. Requirements: the class's own doc comments, Microsoft's published Equals and GetHashCode contract, and RFC 8259. Tests: 43 on this class. 37 C# files under the engine's Source/Programs name this class.
  • osu!, a shipped rhythm game (ppy/osu, MIT, commit 845336e), ScoreProcessor.cs and HitResult.cs. Requirements: their own doc comments. Tests: the 151 test cases in osu.Game.Tests/Rulesets/Scoring. The project has many more, which this pass did not run per break: see below.

Unreal's source is available to anyone with an Unreal licence, not to the general public, so this file gives counts, method names and calls we wrote, and no engine code.

Check it yourself: three faults, each against a rule anyone can read

  • Unreal's SemVer class (Engine/Source/Programs/Shared/EpicGames.Core/SemVer.cs): var v = SemVer.Parse("1.0.0-x-y-z.--"); v.CompareTo(v); throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException. The SemVer spec, rule 9, lists that version among its valid examples. Re-run on the installed 5.7 source on 3 November.
  • Unreal's JsonObject: x.Equals(x) on {"a":null} throws NullReferenceException. Microsoft's Object.Equals contract says x.Equals(x) returns true and that Equals must not throw. Re-run on the installed 5.7 source on 3 November.
  • osu!'s ScoreProcessor: before anything is judged, TotalScoreWithoutMods reads 1,000,000 while TotalScore reads 0. Its own doc comment says it is the points awarded. Re-run on a fresh clone at that commit on 3 November.

The numbers

A break here is a planted bug: one small change to the code on purpose, a mutant in mutation testing, made on its own copy and run against the tests. "Live" leaves out breaks that did not compile and breaks whose compiled code was proven identical to the original. "Caught" means a test failed; "got past" means every test still passed.

SemVer

  • Coverage tool, for comparison: 90% of lines, 85% of branches.
  • 246 breaks made; 236 live; 206 caught (87.3%); 30 got past every test.
  • 14 of those 30 sit on lines the coverage tool marks as covered.
  • 48 of 68 statements held by a test; 18 have a break that gets past.
  • 7 of the 16 requirements taken from the spec have no test about them, including every rule about which strings are valid. Which test is about what was our reading of each test, written before any break ran.

The 30 planted bugs no test caught, by line

Every one is in Engine/Source/Programs/Shared/EpicGames.Core/SemVer.cs as it ships in Unreal Engine 5.7, and every line number below was matched against that file. Each was one change, on its own copy, and the class's 2 tests (PrecedenceTests and PrereleaseTests, in EpicGames.Core.Tests) still passed. To check one, make that change in your own copy and run those tests: none fails. No engine code is printed here, only where each bug was and what changed.

  • Parse: line 54: argument 1 of the call to ArgumentException replaced by its default value; line 54: the statement deleted.
  • TryParse: line 68: the if condition forced to true; line 76: false changed to true.
  • GetHashCode: line 81: argument 2 of the call to AsSpan replaced by its default value; line 81: argument 1 of the call to GetHashCode replaced by its default value; line 81: argument 2 of the call to GetHashCode replaced by its default value; line 81: the constant 0 changed to 1; line 81: the value it returns replaced by its type's default.
  • Equals: line 84: argument 1 of the call to Equals replaced by its default value; line 84: the value it returns replaced by its type's default.
  • CompareTo: line 90: argument 1 of the call to Compare replaced by its default value; line 90: argument 2 of the call to Compare replaced by its default value; line 90: the value it returns replaced by its type's default.
  • ToString: line 93: the value it returns replaced by its type's default.
  • Compare: line 106: argument 2 of the call to GetField replaced by its default value; line 107: argument 2 of the call to GetField replaced by its default value; line 142: the second < on the line changed to <=; line 155: the constant 1 changed to 2.
  • CompareFields: line 175: argument 1 of the call to IsNumeric replaced by its default value; line 175: the if condition forced to true; line 177: argument 1 of the call to IsNumeric replaced by its default value; line 177: the constant 1 changed to 2; line 181: the constant 1 changed to 2.
  • IsNumeric: line 192: the constant 0 changed to 1; line 194: the first < on the line changed to <=; line 194: the first > on the line changed to >=.
  • operator!=: line 210: argument 1 of the call to Equals replaced by its default value; line 210: the value it returns replaced by its type's default.
  • operator<=: line 220: the constant 0 changed to 1.

JsonObject

  • Coverage tool: 77% of lines, 69% of branches.
  • 582 breaks made; 429 live; 299 caught (69.7%); 130 got past every test.
  • 67 of those 130 sit on lines the coverage tool marks as covered.
  • 176 of 289 statements held by a test; 82 have a break that gets past.
  • 6 questions only the class's owner can answer.

osu! scoring

  • Coverage tool, from those 151 tests: 72% of lines, 78% of branches.
  • 563 breaks made; 536 live; 286 caught (53.4%); 250 got past those 151 tests.
  • 145 of those 250 sit on lines the coverage tool marks as covered.
  • 81 of 191 statements held by those tests; 110 have a break that gets past.
  • Read 53.4% as what those three test files hold, and as low for the game as a whole. We applied 7 of the surviving breaks by hand and ran the rest of osu.Game.Tests: TestFailScore, TestResetFromReplayFrame and AccuracyRankAndTotalScoreOfLazerScorePreserved catch some of them. We could not finish that project on this machine: its test host crashed on the clean copy and the broken one, at different points, with and without the visual tests, so what the rest of it would catch is unknown.
  • This pass ran before property bodies were walked, so 5 statements in property bodies got no break.

Checking the tool's verdicts without the tool

We applied breaks the tool said no test notices, by hand, to clean copies, and ran the tests ourselves.

  • SemVer: 6 breaks at once (including CompareTo always answering "equal" and TryParse no longer testing the match): all 90 tests that run still pass, 1 is skipped. No other test project names the class.
  • JsonObject: 8 breaks, each alone, against both test projects that name the class. 7 pass everywhere: RemoveField removes nothing, Equals answers true for anything, GetHashCode is always zero, the file reader stops skipping a byte order mark, the file reader stops skipping comments, Parse refuses trailing commas, a missing double field answers true.
  • The 8th is the tests' credit. JSON false reading as true passes the class's own project, but UnrealBuildTool.Tests catches it. We had first read that as uncaught, and running the second project corrected us.
  • 8 of UnrealBuildTool.Tests' 116 tests fail on the clean copy in our setup, so they could catch nothing here.

What it found

Each of these fails when run, on the code as shipped.

SemVer against the spec

  • Compare throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException on valid versions, including the spec's own example compared with itself: v = SemVer.Parse("1.0.0-x-y-z.--"); v.CompareTo(v);. Any pre-release ending in a hyphen does the same.
  • A hyphen is treated as a separator, but the spec separates identifiers only at dots. 1.0.0-alpha-10 sorts above 1.0.0-alpha-9 (the spec says below). 1.0.0-2 sorts above 1.0.0-1-2 (below).
  • 1.0.0-a.b and 1.0.0-a-b compare as equal while Equals says they differ.
  • It accepts strings the spec rules out: "1.0.0\n", and non-ASCII digits such as an Arabic-Indic zero in 1٠.0.0. Both come from .NET's meaning of $ and \d in the spec's regular expression.
  • Reach: no other C# file under the install's Source/Programs or Plugins names this class, so nothing in that tree is hurt today.

JsonObject against Microsoft's contract

  • Equals throws NullReferenceException on any object with a null field, even x.Equals(x). The contract says it must not throw, and that x.Equals(x) is true.
  • Two objects that compare equal have different hash codes, which the contract forbids. A HashSet of two equal objects holds 2. We found no HashSet<JsonObject> or Dictionary<JsonObject, ...> in the engine's C#.

osu! against its doc comments

  • TotalScoreWithoutMods reads 1,000,000 right after ApplyBeatmap, while TotalScore reads 0, and PopulateScore before the first hit copies that 1,000,000 into the score. The field's doc says "The total number of points awarded for the score without including mod multipliers", and Reset's doc says "Resets this ScoreProcessor to a default state", but Reset never clears it. We did not trace what the game does with the value afterwards.
  • After a second ApplyBeatmap on one processor, MinimumAccuracy reads 1 before any hit. We did not check whether the game ever applies a beatmap twice.

JsonObject: the owner's questions, not defects we can call

  • Equals answers false for two parses of the same text when it holds an array or an object.
  • A repeated name keeps the last value at the top level and throws one level down. {"A":1,"a":2} silently keeps one field, and throws one level down. RFC 8259 only says duplicates are unpredictable between programs.
  • Read accepts comments and Parse refuses them. A root that is not an object throws InvalidOperationException from Read and JsonException from Parse.
  • {"a":1e999} parses, then ToJsonString throws. {"id":9007199254740993} writes back as ...992, which RFC 8259 allows.
  • TryGetIntegerField accepts the string "12". TryGetEnumField<DayOfWeek> accepts "99". On a German machine TryGetDoubleField reads the string "1.5" as 15.

What it found nothing on

  • SemVer: 13 valid strings taken from the spec, 15 of the 19 invalid strings we tried, the printed precedence chain, and build metadata were all correct. All 21 breaks of GetField and all 6 of CompareNumericFields were caught.
  • JsonObject: ToSystemJsonObject (8 of 8 caught), ToJsonNode (10 of 10), Read (5 of 5), ContainsField (3 of 3). A 562 KB file with long escaped strings read correctly, and from that we judged the pooled buffer in Read latent. That was wrong, as the faults below show: "all breaks of Read caught" did not mean Read was right.
  • osu!: all 41 breaks of the nine HitResult questions the tests ask about (IsHit, IsBonus, AffectsCombo and the like) were caught, and so were all 8 of ApplyBeatmap, all 11 of updateScoreMultiplier and all 5 of GetComboScoreChange. By hand, a reverted hit put the score, combo and accuracy back, and each rank's cutoff gave that rank.

Who found what

Be accurate about this. The defects above were found by an agent reading the code against each rule while writing the model: the requirements step. The breaks did not find them. The breaks measured how much the tests hold, and showed where no test looks: 9 breaks of JsonObject.Equals got past every test, and that is where the crash was. No graph neural network (GNN) played a part in any finding here.

More faults, found by reading the code carefully, each proven by the harness on the code as shipped:

  • Read and TryRead parse a file over 128 KiB from a pooled buffer they have already returned. A valid 173 KB file with a very long name came back with other fields silently replaced, while Parse of the same text read it correctly, and a second file made Read throw FormatException.
  • Name matching uses a culture comparer, so names that are different strings can count as one field.
  • RemoveField and AddOrSetFieldValue ignore the empty name, which RFC 8259 allows.
  • NaN and infinity can be set, and then ToJsonString cannot write them. An object parsed 64 levels deep cannot be written either: it reports a cycle that is not there.
  • TryGetEnumField throws on a struct that is not an enum.
  • CreateDeepCopy shares reference values it does not know how to copy, and throws on keys that differ by case and on a multi-dimensional array.

What went badly

The trial's biggest finding was in our own tool. Real code broke it five ways on the first attempts, and a sixth way on osu!, none of which our own examples had shown:

  • It silently skipped code. Any method with overloads, any operator, any generic method with a where clause and any property body was left out, and the report still read as if the whole file was held. On SemVer it saw 35 of 68 statements, missing the private Compare that does all the comparing. On JsonObject it saw 213 of 288.
  • It crashed on read-only files, which is how a Perforce workspace keeps them, on the first run.
  • It mistook a nested type's constructor for a method, and stopped.
  • One mutant with broken braces stopped the whole run.
  • An endless loop in a mutant tested alone hung the run: 11 minutes on one test host before we killed it.

It also could not read MSTest or xUnit tests' /// CHECKS: lines, only NUnit's, and it took a parameterized test's arguments for part of its name, so it reported named tests as never run. Because that fix came after osu!'s pass, its per-requirement check results are not quoted here. All of these are fixed, each with a planted test. A field's value and an indexer are still not walked, and the report now names them.

Our earlier figures on a game feature of ours came through nearly unchanged, because that code has no overloads: no existing verdict changed, and its 7 new breaks found one real gap, which a test now closes.

The budget did not hold. We set 45 minutes and 150K tokens per trial and spent about 100 minutes and over 260K output tokens, most of it on the tool's own bugs. A full pass took 13 minutes on SemVer, 9 on JsonObject and 74 on osu! (each constructor break rebuilds the game), at low priority on a busy machine. The earlier-budgeted 60 minutes for osu! did not hold either.

Re-running it

The models are in t7/ beside this file. For the Unreal trials, copy EpicGames.Core, EpicGames.Core.Tests and their props files from your own engine to a scratch folder and run closed_loop.py on the model; numbers may differ on another engine version, and these are from 5.7. For osu!, clone ppy/osu at commit 845336e, keep the three test files under osu.Game.Tests/Rulesets/Scoring, and run it the same way.
